title: BAR U1·W1 — Ratio & Financial-Statement Analysis (CPA Discipline)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — reading the company through its ratios

The CPA BAR discipline (Business Analysis & Reporting) is where the analysis skills from the CMA program become an exam section. It reuses the most construction content of any discipline — WIP, working capital, and ratios — so MBG is the perfect lens. This week turns the financial statements into ratios that reveal liquidity, efficiency, solvency, and profitability, and decomposes return with the DuPont model.

Liquidity ratios

Liquidity measures the ability to pay short-term obligations. The current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities (a contractor wants comfortably above 1.0, often 1.2–1.5 for bonding). The quick (acid-test) ratio = (current assets − inventory − prepaids) ÷ current liabilities, a sterner test that strips slow assets. The cash ratio uses only cash and equivalents. Working capital (current assets − current liabilities) is the absolute-dollar cushion sureties scrutinize before bonding a job.

Activity ratios and the cash cycle

Activity ratios gauge how efficiently assets are used. Receivables turnover = net credit sales ÷ average receivables, converted to days sales outstanding (DSO) = 365 ÷ turnover. Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ average inventory, converted to days inventory. Payables turnover gives days payable. Combine them into the operating cycle (DSO + days inventory) and the cash conversion cycle (operating cycle − days payable) — the number of days cash is tied up before a job's costs are recovered, a central liquidity driver for a builder financing work in progress.

Solvency and leverage

Solvency measures long-run ability to meet obligations. Debt-to-equity = total liabilities ÷ total equity and debt-to-assets = total liabilities ÷ total assets gauge leverage. Times interest earned = EBIT ÷ interest expense shows how comfortably operating earnings cover interest, and the debt-service-coverage ratio extends that to principal-plus-interest. Sureties and lenders cap a contractor's leverage because a thinly capitalized builder cannot absorb a problem job.

Profitability

Profitability ratios scale earnings to sales or capital. Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue, operating margin = operating income ÷ revenue, and net margin = net income ÷ revenue. Return on assets (ROA) = net income ÷ average assets, return on equity (ROE) = net income ÷ average equity, and return on invested capital (ROIC) measures after-tax operating return on debt-plus-equity capital. For a contractor, gross margin by job type is the most actionable — it isolates estimating and field execution.

The DuPont decomposition

The DuPont model breaks ROE into three levers: ROE = net profit margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier (profitability × efficiency × leverage). Worked example: if MBG earns a 5% net margin, turns assets 2.0 times, and carries an equity multiplier (assets ÷ equity) of 2.5, then ROE = 5% × 2.0 × 2.5 = 25%. The power of the decomposition is diagnostic: a high ROE driven by leverage rather than margin is riskier, and DuPont tells you which lever is doing the work.

Construction-specific analysis

A contractor's statements carry accounts general analysis ignores. Costs and estimated earnings in excess of billings (underbillings) is an asset signaling work performed but not yet billed; billings in excess of costs (overbillings) is a liability signaling the job is billed ahead of cost — generally the healthier financing position. The backlog (signed but unperformed work) predicts future revenue, and the ratio of working capital and equity to backlog is exactly what a surety tests to set bonding capacity. Underbillings that grow faster than revenue can warn of estimating problems or unapproved change orders — a red flag the analyst learns to chase.

Horizontal, vertical, and common-size analysis

Ratios gain meaning in context. Horizontal (trend) analysis compares line items across periods to spot direction; vertical analysis expresses each line as a percentage of a base (sales for the income statement, total assets for the balance sheet); and common-size statements let you compare MBG to a larger competitor despite different scale. The analyst always asks for a benchmark — prior periods, industry medians, or covenant thresholds — because a ratio alone is just a number until it is compared. The standard caveats apply: ratios rely on historical cost, can be distorted by accounting choices, and must be read together, never in isolation.

Market and valuation ratios

Investors layer market ratios on top of the operating ratios. Earnings per share (EPS) drives the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio (market price ÷ EPS), the headline valuation multiple. The dividend yield (dividend per share ÷ price) and the dividend payout ratio (dividends ÷ net income) describe distribution policy, while the retention ratio (1 − payout) feeds sustainable growth. Book value per share and the price-to-book ratio compare market and accounting value, and enterprise-value multiples such as EV/EBITDA value the whole capital structure rather than just equity. A privately held contractor has no market price, so analysts apply these multiples from comparable public companies (with discounts) to estimate value — the same comparable-company logic used to value MBG for a sale or an owner buy-in.

Quality of earnings and the limits of ratios

Ratios are only as good as the earnings beneath them, so the analyst probes quality of earnings. Net income built on aggressive accruals — recognizing revenue early, under-reserving, capitalizing costs that should be expensed — diverges from cash flow, so a persistent gap between net income and operating cash flow is a warning sign. One-time gains, changes in accounting estimates, and off-balance-sheet arrangements can flatter a ratio without improving the business. The disciplined analyst reconciles earnings to cash, strips out nonrecurring items, reads the notes and segment data, and benchmarks against peers — because a single ratio, divorced from cash quality and context, can mislead as easily as inform. For a contractor, the classic distortion is an optimistic estimated cost to complete that inflates percentage-of-completion profit; the analyst tests it against physical progress and change-order history.

Cash-flow-based metrics

Because earnings can be managed, analysts lean on cash. Free cash flow (operating cash flow − capital expenditures) measures the cash a business actually generates after sustaining itself, and operating-cash-flow ratios (operating cash flow ÷ current liabilities, or ÷ total debt) test solvency without accrual noise. The cash-flow-to-net-income ratio gauges earnings quality directly. For a contractor whose reported profit depends on percentage-of-completion estimates, these cash-based measures are an essential cross-check on the accrual story.

CMA bridge

CMA month 7 introduced these same ratios and the DuPont model for internal performance; BAR tests them at exam depth and adds the construction-specific WIP and bonding analysis. The under/overbilling accounts trace straight back to the CMA cost-management and FAR revenue-recognition units — here they become analytical signals.

Practice and recap

  1. Compute liquidity (current, quick, cash, working capital) and read them against bonding thresholds.
  2. Build the operating and cash conversion cycles from DSO, days inventory, and days payable.
  3. Assess leverage (debt-to-equity, times interest earned) and profitability (margins, ROA, ROE, ROIC).
  4. Decompose ROE with DuPont (margin × turnover × leverage) and layer in construction WIP/backlog analysis.

Recap: ratios convert the statements into signals — liquidity and the cash conversion cycle for short-term health, leverage and coverage for solvency, margins and returns for profitability — and DuPont splits a 25% ROE into margin (5%), turnover (2.0), and leverage (2.5) so you can see which lever drives it; for a contractor, underbillings, overbillings, and backlog add the bonding lens a general analysis would miss, while cash-based measures like free cash flow guard against earnings flattered by optimistic percentage-of-completion estimates.
